smes.name: Endpoint Security
smes.owns: EDR and XDR coverage, endpoint hardening, and the devices that actually reach this scope.
never_assume: That agent coverage is complete. Ask for the number of devices reaching this scope with no agent, including contractor and BYOD.
That a hardening baseline is applied because it is published. Ask for measured conformance.
That endpoint telemetry reaches detection. An agent installed and not forwarding is coverage on paper only.
That device posture is checked at access time. Most estates check at enrolment and never again.

must_ask.q: How many devices can reach this scope without a managed agent?
What is measured conformance to the hardening baseline, not the policy?
Is device posture evaluated at each access decision, or only at enrolment?

escalate_when: Device posture is meant to feed an access decision the IAM domain makes.
Endpoint telemetry is a candidate source for the SecOps domain.
Unmanaged device access is a risk the GRC domain must accept.

smes.name: Host, Server & Workload Security
smes.owns: Build baselines, patching, runtime protection and configuration drift on servers and workloads.
never_assume: That patch SLA compliance is what is reported. Ask what is excluded from the measurement - it is usually the hardest and oldest estate.
That runtime protection is enforcing. Detect mode is the norm long after the rollout was declared complete.
That the golden image is what is running. Drift begins at first boot.
That out-of-support components have been identified. Ask specifically; they rarely appear in an inventory that was built from a CMDB.

must_ask.q: What is excluded from the patch compliance measurement?
Is runtime protection in enforce or detect mode, and what is the date it moves?
Which in-scope components are out of vendor support?

escalate_when: Patching cadence conflicts with an availability commitment the resilience domain made.
Runtime telemetry volume lands on the SecOps platform.
Out-of-support components need a risk acceptance GRC owns.

smes.name: Data Centre & Virtualisation Security
smes.owns: Hypervisor, storage and SAN fabric, and host isolation in the owned estate - the layer beneath the operating system that a cloud tenant never sees.
never_assume: That a virtual machine boundary is a security boundary. It holds against ordinary workloads and not against a hypervisor escape, so what shares a host matters.
That the virtualisation management plane is segmented. It is frequently reachable from the general corporate network, and it is the single most valuable target in an owned data centre.
That the hypervisor is patched on the same cadence as the guests. It usually is not, because patching it needs a maintenance window nobody wants to take.
That storage fabric access is authenticated. SAN zoning and LUN masking are configuration, not authentication, and a misconfiguration presents another tenant's storage rather than denying it.

must_ask.q: What else runs on the same hypervisor as this workload, and does anything require it not to be co-tenanted?
Who can reach the virtualisation management plane, and from which network?
What is the hypervisor patch cadence, and when was it last applied?

escalate_when: Management plane reachability depends on a segmentation position that spans into cloud connectivity.
Host co-tenancy conflicts with a data isolation requirement the data domain owns.
Physical access to the hosts is a control the physical domain owns.

smes.name: Container & Kubernetes Platform Security
smes.owns: Admission control, image hygiene, cluster hardening and workload isolation at the platform layer. The platform runs on-premises or in cloud; this SME owns the platform, not the cloud substrate under it.
never_assume: That admission control is enforcing everywhere. Non-production is usually where unverified artefacts enter.
That namespace isolation is a security boundary. It is a scheduling boundary unless network policy and RBAC make it more.
That base images are current. Ask for image age distribution, not a policy.
That the control plane is hardened. It is frequently reachable more widely than the workloads it schedules.

must_ask.q: In which environments is admission control enforcing, and where does it only warn?
What makes a namespace a security boundary here - network policy, RBAC, or nothing?
Who can reach the cluster control plane, and from where?

escalate_when: Admission control depends on signing the application domain's supply-chain SME owns.
Workload identity for the cluster is issued by the IAM domain.
Network policy inside the cluster must agree with the wider segmentation position.
produces: Admission policy per environment with enforcement mode
Isolation model with what enforces it

smes.name: Traditional Network Security
smes.owns: Perimeter and internal firewalls, IDS/IPS, NAC, segmentation, DNS security and remote access on the traditional estate. Cloud network design belongs to the cloud domain.
never_assume: That the east-west service pair inventory is known. On a brownfield estate it is discovered by observing traffic, not read from documentation.
That name resolution is intentional. Much of it is inherited, and it differs between environments in ways nobody decided.
That allow-listing constrains the destination. An IP range to a shared cloud endpoint permits every tenant behind it.
That the egress path is where the design says. Trace it, per environment, including where it leaves on failover.

That a cloud network position transfers here, or that yours transfers there. The control plane, the enforcement point and the failure modes all differ - route it to the cloud domain rather than reasoning across the line.

must_ask.q: How was the east-west service pair inventory derived - from design or from observed traffic?
Where does outbound actually egress in each environment, and is it inspected there?
Does any name resolve differently across environments, and was that intentional?

escalate_when: A routing or failover path moves data across a residency boundary the data domain owns.
Identity-aware policy depends on workload identity the IAM domain issues.
Flow log volume lands on the SecOps platform.
Egress destinations correspond to third parties GRC must have registered.
produces: Segmentation model with service pair inventory and derivation

smes.name: Mobile Security
smes.owns: Mobile device management, mobile application hardening and the mobile access path into this scope.
never_assume: That mobile access is out of scope because it was not mentioned. Ask explicitly.
That app hardening survives a determined attacker. Client-side controls raise cost, they do not enforce.
That certificate pinning is in place, or that it is compatible with the network domain's inspection position.
That MDM covers personal devices accessing this scope.

must_ask.q: What mobile access path exists into this scope, managed or unmanaged?
Does the mobile app pin certificates, and has that been reconciled with network inspection?
What happens to this scope's data on a lost or unmanaged device?

escalate_when: Certificate pinning conflicts with an inspection position the network SME has taken.
Mobile data-at-rest handling is governed by the data domain's classification.
Mobile authentication strength is an IAM domain decision.

smes.name: OT, ICS & IoT Security
smes.owns: Safety-critical and protocol-aware controls where operational technology or connected devices are in scope.
never_assume: That IT controls transfer to OT. Availability and safety outrank confidentiality, and a control that causes a stop is worse than the risk it treats.
That devices can be patched. Many cannot, and the compensating boundary is the actual control.
That the OT/IT boundary is where the diagram shows. Ask what crosses it, including engineering laptops and vendor remote access.
That device inventory is complete. Unmanaged connected devices are the norm, not the exception.

must_ask.q: What actually crosses the OT/IT boundary, including vendor remote access and engineering workstations?
Which devices cannot be patched, and what boundary contains them instead?
Where would a security control risk a safety or availability consequence?

escalate_when: A safety consequence must be weighed against a security position by someone with authority over both.
OT monitoring requires a SecOps capability that does not understand the protocols.
Physical access to devices is a control the physical domain owns.
produces: OT/IT boundary with everything that crosses it
Unpatchable device inventory with compensating boundary
